subject: Beginner's question on latent Gaussian field and Gaussian approximation to its full conditional

messages.author: b91e54f3020c0cfd
messages.subject: Beginner's question on latent Gaussian field and Gaussian approximation to its full conditional
parts:
Dear INLA people,

I am currently starting to look into INLA for using it on models for pathogen dispersal in plant ecology.
I would first like to thank the creators and maintainers of the R-INLA site for their great work!

After working through several INLA papers, I now have a rather theoretical question about the construction of the latent gaussian vector x and the gaussian approximation of pi(x|y,theta), using the Rue, Martino, Chopin 2009 (RMC in the following) notations.
I have a small toy example (which, of course, is not necessarily a „good“ model in practice) that I want to implement by myself and which should be useful to explain the points that I do not understand or that I possibly misunderstand.
Here's the model:

eta = mu + z
mu normal variable with precision tau_mu
z  a normal random vector (of length 100, for instance) with diagonal precision matrix with entries tau_z
mu and z are assumed to be independent
y_i Poisson distributed according to exp(eta_i)

I could think of two possible parametrizations of x: either x=(eta,mu) or x=(z,mu)
Following RMC Section 2.2, we want the conditional distribution of y_i to depend only on one single x_i, so we should use the x=(eta,mu) parametrization (?). Otherwise, y_i would depend on z_i and mu, leading to complications in the Newton-Raphson algorithm used to get the Gaussian approximation and leading to a non-sparse precision matrix  in the approximation due to dependence of y_i on z_i and mu (?).
Now with Cov(mu, eta_i) = Cov(mu,mu) = tau_mu^{-1}, we get a sparse covariance matrix for x,
with nonzero entries on the diagonal and in the last row and the last column.
However, the precision matrix would then not be sparse, contrary to what is desired for applying INLA.
How could this problem be avoided?
In the mode x*(theta) of the full conditional pi(x|y,theta), what do we take for mu*? There is no observation y_i directly associated to mu, so I am not sure how it has to be treated. Would it be necessary or useful to impose some linear constraints on x? (like mean(eta_i)=mu ?)

Thanks for your comments and elucidation on these questions.

Best,

Thomas

Hi

what we do, is to work with

x = (eta, mu, z)

defined so that

eta | mu,z ~ N( ``mu + z'', I*high.precision)

so the joint is non-singular.

then sparsity is ok ;-)

Best
H

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Beginner's question on latent Gaussian field and Gaussian approximation to its full conditional
parts:
On 08/01/15 10:47, Thomas Opitz wrote:
> I could think of two possible parametrizations of x: either x=(eta,mu)
> or x=(z,mu)

Like Håvard just replied, R+INLA uses a third option, but it's worth
saying a few more words on this topic. In the model you describe, the
(eta, mu) parameterisation would actually be just fine, and would not
generate dense precisions; it's the _covariance_ that becomes dense.

eta_i = mu + z_i
Prec(mu) = tau_mu
Prec(z) = tau_z I, number of z_i:s is n_z
y_i ~ Po(exp(eta_i))

The joint precision for eta and mu is a block matrix
[tau_z I, -tau_z 1;
-tau_z 1^T, tau_mu + n_z tau_z]
(since the _conditional_ precision for eta given mu is the same as the
_marginal_ precision for the z-vector)

In the Newton optimisation, the contribution from the data likelihood
(via the second order derivatives) only affects the diagonal (only the
upper left diagonal block), and the precision sparsity stays sparse.

In addition, using the (z, mu) parameterisation would _also_ be ok for
this stage! In this model, the latent model precision would be
[tau_z I, 0;
0, tau_mu]
and the observation model y_i ~ Po(exp(mu + z_i)) would affect the
diagonal, but also the final row and the final column.
(d^2 / dz_i dz_j of the log-likelihood is zero when i \neq j, so they
don't contribute).
The resulting sparsity will therefore be the same as in the (eta, mu)
parameterisation, and the Newton step would work in exactly the same
way as there.

It's the later steps of the INLA method that really needs the "may use
only one element of eta" restriction. The Newton step is fine as long
as the sparsity structure of the observation dependence on eta is
similar to that of the latent model itself, and this is why the
extended representation shown by Håvard is used in the general
implementation, even though in this special case, (eta, mu) would
have also fulfilled the restriction.

Finn
